review_basis: Individually inspected original numbered Module 12 WebP slides 01–05 at full resolution. Narration begins with the visual purpose, walks every meaningful panel/arrow/decision and the actual bottom worked example, then connects the parts as one picture; no PDF-title substitution.
part_title: IAM Identities, Policies, Permission Evaluation and Service Roles

scenes.title: IAM: Users and Groups
scenes.visual_overview: How an AWS account separates the powerful root identity from ordinary users, and how group policies determine team access to services.
visual_walkthrough: Root-user panel: full account privileges, rare tasks and MFA
Users Alice, Bob, Carlos and Diana flow into Developers and Audit groups
Different developer and read-only audit policies point to EC2, S3 and RDS
Four-stage worked example: create users, create groups, assign membership, attach policies
Exam cue: identities, groups, root-user restrictions and least privilege
scenes.visual_example: Alice and Bob receive developer-group access; Carlos and Diana receive audit group read-only access.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Use individual/federated identities and grouped least-privilege policies; reserve root for rare account operations.
scenes.narration: This visual introduces the starting point of AWS access control: who is signing in, how we organize people into teams, and how those teams receive just enough permission to work. Begin with the separate red panel on the left. The AWS account root identity exists when the account is created and has unusually broad power. Protect it with multi-factor authentication, or MFA, and reserve it for exceptional account tasks; it is not an everyday developer login. Now follow the larger diagram from left to right. Alice, Bob, Carlos and Diana are individual IAM users. The blue arrows place Alice and Bob in the developers group, while the purple arrows place Carlos and Diana in the audit group. A group contains users; it is not itself the identity making the API request. Next, each group receives a different policy. The developers policy allows only the actions needed for development on services such as EC2 and S3. The audit policy gives read-only access for reviewing information, illustrated by Amazon RDS, without permission to modify it. Notice that the permissions are about specific actions, not simply seeing an AWS service icon. The four boxes along the bottom repeat the actual setup sequence: create users, create the two groups, assign the people, then attach the appropriate policies. The full picture is about separating identities from job-based permissions. For real workforce access, centralized federation and temporary credentials are generally preferable; whatever identity approach you choose, the principle shown here remains least privilege.

scenes.title: IAM Permissions and Policy Evaluation
scenes.visual_overview: How AWS evaluates an action request through identity grants and applicable limits before returning allow or deny.
visual_walkthrough: Analyst requests an AWS resource action
Identity policy, permissions boundary, session policy, Organizations SCP/RCP limit boxes
Decision tree: explicit deny, identity allow, remaining applicable limits
Right-hand results: explicit deny, implicit no-allow and limit-based denial
Worked S3 GetObject policy with marketing-dataset allowed and finance-dataset denied
Bottom exam cue on explicit deny and scoped permissions
scenes.visual_example: The policy permits s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::marketing-dataset/* but not the finance-dataset object, assuming no other grants and all limits allow.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Access requires an applicable allow without an explicit deny or blocking boundary; the slide uses a simplified identity-based example.
scenes.narration: This slide answers an important question: when an analyst asks AWS to read a file, why is one request allowed while another is rejected? Follow the three numbered areas across the top. First, the analyst requests an action on a resource. Second, AWS evaluates the relevant rules. The blue list shows identity-based policies that grant or deny actions, plus permissions boundaries, session policies and AWS Organizations service or resource control policies where applicable. A boundary or session policy is a limit on permissions; attaching a broad allow does not simply bypass it. Now trace the decision flow in the third panel. The red branch asks whether any applicable rule explicitly denies the request. If yes, the request is denied, even if another policy says allow. If not, this simplified identity-policy example looks for an explicit allow. Without one, the grey box shows an implicit denial. With an allow, AWS still checks all applicable limits; a restrictive boundary, session policy or Organizations control can prevent access. Only when the allow and those constraints line up do we reach the green result. The worked example beneath is concrete. The JSON permits the action s3:GetObject for objects under the marketing-dataset bucket, written as its object ARN followed by a star. The green row shows marketing-dataset/file.csv allowed; the red row shows finance-dataset/file.csv denied because it lies outside that scope. This example assumes no other grants; resource-based permissions can follow additional evaluation rules. The big-picture lesson is that authorizing a request means checking both what is granted and what can still block it.

scenes.title: IAM Policy Inheritance
scenes.visual_overview: How a user's direct policies and every group membership contribute permissions, with denies and boundaries still limiting the result.
visual_walkthrough: Alice as the IAM user on the left
Three arrows to attached user policies, group policies and inline user policy
Merge into effective permissions on the right
Explicit deny and other applicable controls panel
Bottom worked example combines user, Developers, ReadOnly and inline permissions
Exam cue: group grants, inline policy, union of allows subject to limits
scenes.visual_example: Alice combines ec2:DescribeInstances and s3:ListBucket from a direct policy, Lambda and CloudWatch Logs rights from Developers, S3 and DynamoDB read rights from ReadOnly, and ssm:StartSession from an inline user policy.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Grant sources add applicable allows; explicit denies and other policy boundaries remain in force.
scenes.narration: Here we extend the previous slide by looking at where one person's permissions come from. The image asks what happens when Alice receives permissions from several places at once. Start with Alice on the left and follow the three colored arrows. The upper arrow leads to policies attached directly to her IAM user, which may be managed or inline. The middle arrow leads to policies on every group she belongs to; a user can belong to multiple groups. The lower arrow highlights one inline user policy, a policy embedded in that particular identity rather than a reusable managed-policy attachment. These boxes represent sources of permission, not three mandatory processing stages. All three arrows join before the effective-permissions panel on the right. Its green result includes the applicable allows, but the red explicit-deny box overrides any matching grant. Permissions boundaries, Organizations controls, session policies and applicable resource policies also affect the final decision. Let's read the worked example across the bottom. Alice's direct policy permits EC2 instance descriptions and S3 bucket listing. The Developers group adds Lambda invocation and creating CloudWatch log groups. The ReadOnly group adds reading S3 objects and describing DynamoDB tables. The inline policy adds starting an SSM session. Those illustrated actions form the combined candidate permissions, unless a deny or another control blocks them. An important distinction: IAM groups contain users but cannot be nested inside one another. The overall picture is that multiple policy sources can add rights, but effective access is still the outcome of the full AWS policy evaluation.

scenes.title: IAM Policy Structure
scenes.visual_overview: How an identity-based IAM JSON policy identifies allowed or denied API actions, resources and optional conditions.
visual_walkthrough: Left attachment targets: IAM users, groups and roles; groups are not request principals
Center field reference: Version, Statement, Effect, Action, Resource, optional Condition
Right service/resource path: S3 and bucket/object scope
Bottom sample JSON and color-coded arrows to actual fields
Principal warning and exam cue on scoped ARNs
scenes.visual_example: JSON uses Version 2012-10-17, Effect Allow, Actions s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, and both a bucket ARN and an object ARN.
scenes.visual_synthesis: IAM authorization depends on action and resource ARN combinations; Principal belongs in resource or trust policies rather than standard identity-based policies.
scenes.narration: This slide makes IAM policies less mysterious by showing the actual JSON document that AWS evaluates. A policy is a structured set of permission statements, not a list of names that automatically receive full service access. Start on the left: standard identity-based policies can be attached to users, groups or roles. Groups help organize users, but a group is not the principal making a request. Move to the central field guide. Version describes the IAM policy language and the sample uses 2012-10-17. Statement contains one or more rules. Within a rule, Effect is Allow or Deny, Action names API operations, Resource identifies their scope, and Condition can add restrictions such as network or identity context. Now follow the arrow to Amazon S3 on the right: an action applies to a particular resource type, such as a bucket or an object inside it. The color-coded sample JSON along the bottom makes this concrete. Its Effect is Allow, its two Actions are s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, and its Resource list includes both my-bucket and my-bucket slash star. That difference matters: listing applies to the bucket ARN, while reading objects applies to object ARNs. A broader-looking policy still needs the correct action and resource pair. Finally, read the gold warning. Principal does not appear in a standard identity-based policy; it belongs in resource-based or role trust policies where you identify who can access or assume something. The whole image teaches you to parse a policy by asking: which action, on which resource, under which conditions?

scenes.title: IAM Roles for Services
scenes.visual_overview: How EC2 or Lambda obtains temporary AWS credentials through a service-trusted IAM role rather than hard-coded access keys.
visual_walkthrough: Four numbered top stages: service, trust policy, STS credentials and S3 access
EC2/Lambda icons and AssumeRole arrow to IAM role
Trust-policy JSON with Principal Service ec2.amazonaws.com and sts:AssumeRole
AWS STS short-lived credential box and arrow to S3
S3 permissions JSON limiting GetObject/PutObject to my-app-bucket objects
Bottom EC2 read example and exam cue
scenes.visual_example: An EC2 instance uses an instance profile and an EC2-trusted role, receives temporary credentials, and reads an approved S3 object with s3:GetObject.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Trust policy governs who may assume the role; permissions policy governs what the resulting session can do.
scenes.narration: This image explains a common AWS security pattern: an application running on an EC2 instance or in Lambda needs S3 access, but we should not place a permanent access key inside the code. Follow the four numbered steps across the top. The AWS service is associated with an IAM role. In the second stage, the role's trust policy names the service allowed to assume it. The sample JSON shows the service principal ec2.amazonaws.com and the action sts:AssumeRole; a Lambda role would trust lambda.amazonaws.com instead. Notice how this is different from the identity policy on the previous slide, because a trust policy answers who can assume the role. In step three, AWS Security Token Service provides short-lived credentials, including a session token, which the service receives and refreshes through its AWS integration. The arrow then leads to Amazon S3. The role's separate permissions policy controls what that temporary session may do. The pictured example lists s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject for objects under my-app-bucket, not unrestricted access to every bucket. Now follow the worked example below. An EC2 instance uses a role through its instance profile, the EC2 service is trusted to assume it, temporary credentials become available to the instance, and the workload can call s3:GetObject if permissions allow. The final exam panel stresses three things: service principals differ, credentials are temporary, and action/resource scope still matters. Together, the trust policy and the permissions policy explain the entire flow: who receives credentials and what those credentials authorize.
